issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may not reverse concurrent factual findings by reappreciating evidence where the lower courts considered the relevant evidence and their findings are not shown to be perverse or based on an erroneous approach.
material_facts: The trial court found that the landlord bona fide required the premises for his proposed business and had no other suitable shop available.
The lower appellate court considered the evidence and affirmed the trial court’s finding.
The High Court reversed those concurrent findings after reappreciating the evidence.
The Supreme Court found no showing that the lower courts had failed to consider relevant evidence or had adopted an erroneous approach.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in law by setting aside the concurrent findings of fact through reappreciation of the evidence; the lower courts’ decrees were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principles governing second appeals, an erroneous finding of fact based on appreciation of relevant evidence does not by itself justify interference; a bona fide requirement finding ordinarily turns on appreciation of evidence and does not give rise to a substantial question of law. The Court relied on Kashibai w/o Lachiram v. Parwatibai w/o Lachiram, [1995] 6 SCC 213, and Ram Prasad Rajak v. Nand Kumar & Bros., JT (1998) 5 SC 540. It distinguished Dilbagrai Punjabi v. Sharad Chandra, AIR (1988) SC 1858, and Jagdish Singh v. Natthu Singh, AIR (1992) SC 1604, which permit interference where relevant evidence was not considered or the approach was essentially erroneous.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and relevant_evidence_considered and not demonstrated_perversity_or_erroneous_approach

predicates.second_appeal: The challenged decision was made in a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual finding.
predicates.relevant_evidence_considered: The lower courts considered the relevant evidence in reaching their findings.
predicates.demonstrated_perversity_or_erroneous_app: The record demonstrates that the lower courts’ findings were perverse or resulted from an essentially erroneous approach.

issues.definition: When a second appeal challenges concurrent factual findings made after consideration of the relevant evidence, and no perversity or essentially erroneous approach is demonstrated, reversal through reappreciation is improper.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s bona fide business requirement is not defeated merely because the landlord or family members own other premises where no other premises is shown to be vacant and suitable, and the landlord is best placed to judge the suitability of the premises sought.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction to use the premises for a showroom for businesses for which he had been appointed a sub-dealer.
The trial court found the premises were needed bona fide for the landlord’s business and that no other suitable shop was available to him.
The landlord testified that other shops and houses belonging to him were not vacant and that the disputed premises were suitable for his business.
An amended pleading stated that the buildings left by the landlord’s deceased father were occupied by tenants, belonged to other heirs, and were not vacant or in the landlord’s possession.
The tenant produced no further pleading or evidence after the amendment.
The Supreme Court found nothing on the record showing that any other shop was both vacant and suitable for the proposed business.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent finding of bona fide requirement was supported by the evidence; the landlord’s choice of the premises could not be faulted on the record, and the High Court’s contrary treatment of the alternative premises was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(1)(f) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961, provides the eviction ground for bona fide requirement. The landlord is the best judge of his requirement for residential or business purposes and has complete freedom in that choice; the Court relied on Prativa Devi (Smt.) v. T.K. Krishnan, [1996] 5 SCC 353. The landlord must establish the bona fide requirement, but the evidence here supported that finding and did not establish the existence of other vacant, suitable premises.

predicates.bona_fide_business_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction so that the landlord can use the premises for a proposed business on a claim of bona fide need.
predicates.landlord_established_business_need: The landlord presents evidence establishing a genuine need to use the premises for that business.
predicates.other_premises_not_shown_vacant_and_suit: The evidence does not show that another premises available to the landlord is both vacant and suitable for the proposed business.

issues.definition: When a landlord establishes a genuine business need in an eviction proceeding and no other premises is shown to be both vacant and suitable, the landlord’s choice of suitable premises is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord need not give further evidence after an amendment setting out facts about alternative premises when the opposing party does not rebut the amendment.
material_facts: After the landlord’s father died, the plaint was amended to state that the buildings left by the father were occupied by tenants, belonged to the landlord’s mother and other heirs, and were neither vacant nor in the landlord’s possession.
The tenant filed no additional written statement and neither party adduced further evidence after the amendment.
The High Court faulted the landlord for not giving evidence after the amendment.
issues.conclusion: It was not necessary for the landlord to give further evidence after the amendment because the tenant did not rebut it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the case-specific principle that an amended factual assertion left unrebutted by the opposing party did not require the landlord to give further evidence. The Court relied on the absence of any additional written statement or evidence following the amendment.

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant from premises.
predicates.pleading_amended_with_facts_about_altern: The landlord amends the pleading to state facts about the availability, occupancy, ownership, or possession of alternative premises.
predicates.opposing_party_did_not_rebut_amendment: The opposing party files no responsive pleading or evidence challenging the amended facts.

issues.definition: When an eviction pleading is amended with facts about alternative premises and the opposing party does not rebut those facts, further testimony on the amendment is not required.
